questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify how unequal district sizes distort seat shares.
questions.stem: At the transit authority board, District East has 300,000 residents and two seats while District West has 60,000 residents and also two seats. What follows?

options.text: East residents get far more representation per head than West residents do
Both districts are represented in proportion to their number of residents
options.misconception: assumes seats already track each district's population

options.text: The board becomes malapportioned only when East wins more seats at an election
options.misconception: assumes malapportionment needs a vote outcome to appear

options.text: Seat totals decide representation, so equal seat counts guarantee equal voice
options.misconception: believes seat counts alone settle who holds real power

questions.explanation: Each East councillor speaks for about 150,000 people and a West councillor for 30,000, so seats do not track residents. Equal seat totals still produce unequal voice.
questions.hint: Compare residents per seat, not seat totals.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Equal voice against a majority rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a consent rule protects a minority against a numerical majority.

stimulus.body: The board adopted a rule that a measure affecting routes in one corridor requires the consent of all four corridor delegates, so that no corridor can be outvoted on its own access. A corridor with 40 per cent of riders can therefore block a change that 60 per cent of riders want.

questions.stem: Read the transit board's extract and identify what the arrangement protects.

options.text: The rule guarantees that every rider's weight is identical in every vote
options.misconception: believes a consent rule equalises every individual's vote weight

options.text: The rule guarantees that a numerical majority cannot override a local minority
The rule ensures that the corridor with the most riders always carries the measure
options.misconception: assumes supermajority rules always favour the largest group

options.text: The rule requires unanimity simply because the corridors were drawn at different times
options.misconception: thinks bloc rules depend on the age of the districts

questions.explanation: The consent rule blocks a majority from overriding one corridor, so a minority can veto a change it opposes. It neither equalises individual weight nor favours the largest corridor.
questions.hint: Ask who can stop a measure despite majority support.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how turnout differences change the weight of each ballot cast.
questions.stem: Explain to the transit board why a low turnout in one district can leave its voters with more say per ballot than a high-turnout district, using figures from the last route consultation.

answer.exemplar: Turnout changes the number of votes cast, not the number of seats a district holds. If 100,000 eligible voters turn out in District East against 10,000 in District West, and each district elects two councillors, then each East ballot carries one 10,000th of a seat while each West ballot carries one 5,000th, so the low-turnout district's voters have twice the weight per vote. Representation still depends on where the votes were cast.

questions.explanation: Seat counts are fixed by district, so the same votes buy less representation where turnout is high. Per-ballot weight is inverse to turnout, so low turnout means stronger weight per vote cast.
questions.hint: Seat totals are fixed; only votes cast vary.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the question a run-off is designed to settle.

stimulus.body: After the depot election for chair of the operators' liaison group, no candidate reached 50 per cent. The returning officer has scheduled a second poll between the two leading candidates, to be held in three weeks unless a withdrawal is filed.

questions.stem: In the situation described in the bulletin, what does the second poll primarily resolve?

options.text: The question of whether turnout in the depot will be high enough to matter
options.misconception: assumes a run-off is mainly a test of how many people show up

options.text: The question of whether the chair's election should be delayed for a year
options.misconception: believes a second poll is a device for delaying the result

options.text: The question of which candidate commands majority support among voters
The question of whether all three candidates should be allowed to stay in the race
options.misconception: thinks a run-off is used to widen the field of candidates

questions.explanation: A run-off is triggered when nobody wins a majority, and the second poll pits the two leaders against each other to produce a majority-backed winner. Turnout and field size are secondary.
questions.hint: Name the office no one won on the first count.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a suspicion of a self-serving redraw.
questions.stem: The boundary commission redrew the depot districts right after a party won by two votes in one district. Which reading of that sequence best fits the evidence?

options.text: The redraw was clearly legal because boundaries are set after every election
options.misconception: assumes all post-election redraws are lawful and routine

options.text: The redraw was clearly illegal because no district may ever be redrawn
options.misconception: believes boundaries can never be revised after an election

options.text: The redraw had no political effect because seat totals stayed the same
options.misconception: assumes equal seat totals make a redraw politically neutral

options.text: The narrow win raises suspicion of a self-serving redraw that needs scrutiny

questions.explanation: Redrawing seats immediately after a narrow win can lock in an advantage, so the sequence justifies scrutiny of the new boundaries. The facts do not prove illegality, nor does keeping seat totals make a redraw neutral.

questions.learningObjective: Trace the sequence from representation to executive choice.

options.text: Representation is established first, and executive choice follows from it
Departments choose councillors, and the council then ratifies their choice
options.misconception: reverses the chain by putting hiring before representation

options.text: A single election decides both the council's membership and its policy programme
options.misconception: believes one vote settles membership and policy together

options.text: The chair is chosen first, and the council then fills the vacant council seats
options.misconception: assumes the executive is chosen before the legislature exists

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one member per district shapes who wins a seat.

stimulus.body: In the depot wards, each councillor represents one district and is re-elected every four years. Voters who dislike the winner of their own district can only remove that person by backing someone else inside the same district; they cannot select a different candidate elsewhere.

questions.stem: Using the report extract, identify the limitation of the single-member arrangement described.

options.text: Voters are required to rank candidates across the whole city before a seat is allocated
options.misconception: confuses a ranked citywide ballot with district voting

options.text: The winner of a district takes the seat even when most of the district opposed that person
Each councillor in the depot wards is elected by a majority of the whole city
options.misconception: confuses a district election with a citywide proportional vote

options.text: Voters have no way to express a preference among the candidates in their district
options.misconception: believes voters lose all influence over the choice of candidate

questions.explanation: With one member per district, the largest vote share takes the seat even without a majority, and voters can only act inside their own district. Defeating an unpopular winner needs a local challenger.
questions.hint: Focus on who wins the seat, not who votes most.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a small party can gain leverage from a run-off.
questions.stem: Explain how a small party that wins 8 per cent in a first round can still influence the outcome of a run-off, and what conditions on that party would make the effect stronger.

answer.exemplar: In a first round with no majority, the top two candidates meet in a run-off, so a party with 8 per cent can matter if it is one of the two qualifying candidates. Its influence grows when the top two are close to each other, when its votes are concentrated in districts that swing the run-off, and when the parties that finished behind it would prefer its rival to win. Small parties can also withdraw and endorse a candidate, changing who reaches the second round.

questions.explanation: A run-off between the top two lets a minor party trade support for leverage, especially when it sits just behind the qualifying places. Vote concentration and a close top two magnify it.
questions.hint: Think about the second round and who reaches it.

questions.learningObjective: Compare residents per seat across districts of unequal size.

options.misconception: confuses travel distance to a tram stop with representation weight

options.misconception: believes small electorates gain more from a fixed seat count

options.text: Hill commuters face much heavier representation duties per voter than riverside residents

questions.explanation: Two seats for 12,000 voters gives about 6,000 per councillor against 90,000 in the hill corridor. Travel distance to a tram stop is a service question, not a representation one.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a councillor's constituency from the ballots actually cast.

options.text: The hill ward's councillor represents 1,333 voters and the depot ward's represents 2,500
options.misconception: confuses voters actually polled with the registered electorate

options.text: Each ward's councillor represents 20,000 registered voters regardless of ballots cast
The depot ward's councillor represents 8,000 voters because only they were polled
options.misconception: treats the ballots cast as the size of the represented constituency

options.text: Turnout totals show that the hill ward's councillor is less representative in practice
options.misconception: assumes turnout differences change the legal size of the constituency

stimulus.body: Polls are to be held in the works council election. The returning officer will publish the result of the first poll within three working days.

options.misconception: confuses the candidate list with the qualifying candidates

When the outgoing chair's term of office will come to an end

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out safeguards that insulate a redraw from an election result.
questions.stem: Set out the safeguards a boundary commission can adopt so that a redraw is not shaped by the result of the seat it may affect.

answer.exemplar: A commission can require that boundaries be reviewed on a fixed cycle rather than immediately after a contested election, publish the data and the drafting rules before drafting begins, hold hearings in the affected districts, consult independent experts on the map, and record written reasons for each change. Deciding these procedures in advance removes the incentive to draw a seat around a narrow win and makes the process open to challenge.

questions.explanation: Timing rules, published data, hearings and written reasons reduce the chance of drawing a seat around a narrow margin. They work because they fix the process before the contested result is known.
questions.hint: Fix the process before the contested result exists.

questions.explanation: The calendar puts certification and the first council meeting in week three and the chair's election in week four, so representation must exist before the chair is chosen.

questions.learningObjective: Judge what a near tie produces under a one-member district.

The runner-up should receive a fraction of the seat under a fair reading
options.misconception: believes near-tied districts are entitled to a partial seat

options.text: The ward must repeat the poll because the margin is too small to count
options.misconception: assumes narrow margins automatically trigger a recount poll

options.text: The ward should have elected two councillors to make the result clearer
options.misconception: assumes adding a second seat would remove the winner-take-all effect

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Equal voice against a majority rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a supermajority threshold on board decisions.
questions.stem: Explain what changes and what stays the same when a transit board replaces simple majority voting with a rule requiring a supermajority of all members for a route restructuring.

answer.exemplar: A supermajority rule makes it harder to pass a restructuring, so a small group of members can block a proposal that a simple majority supports, and the status quo survives more often. It also raises the burden on the winning side to build cross-party agreement before voting. What stays the same is the source of authority: members still hold equal votes and the board still decides within the rules it adopted, so legitimacy now depends on the threshold being accepted by the members it binds.

questions.explanation: A supermajority threshold blocks measures a simple majority would carry. Authority stays with the same members, and legitimacy depends on whether they accept the higher threshold.
questions.hint: Separate who decides from how hard it is to win.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Connect two effects of the single-member system to design features.
questions.stem: Explain why a single-member district system is often described as both geographically responsive and resistant to the smaller parties' preferences, and state the design feature responsible for each effect.

answer.exemplar: The system is geographically responsive because each councillor is elected by and answerable to one defined district, so residents know exactly whom to approach about a route or a timetable in their own area. It is resistant to smaller parties because each district returns a single winner by a plurality, so a party with a well-spread but low share of the national vote can win no seats at all. The responsible feature is the combination of one representative per district and a single-name contest that rewards concentrated support.

questions.explanation: One member per district gives every area a named, reachable representative, explaining local responsiveness. A single-name contest rewards concentrated votes, which is why minor parties gain nothing.
questions.hint: Two effects, two design features, one system.

questions.explanation: With twenty votes and a threshold of eleven, a motion needs a strict majority, so a ten-vote block can defeat a ten-vote majority. Equal votes per member do not produce equal chances of winning.

questions.learningObjective: Infer a structured cause of low turnout from a service change.

stimulus.body: Depot wards A and B each have 24,000 registered voters. In ward A, 19,200 ballots were cast; in ward B, 9,600 ballots were cast. A comparative analysis notes that ward A's participation has been stable for five years, while ward B's has fluctuated widely and its low figure coincides with the closure of a nearby evening service.

questions.stem: On the basis of the circular, what is the most useful inference about turnout in ward B?

options.misconception: confuses the size of the electorate with the weight of each ballot

options.text: Ward B's low turnout is simply the result of random variation across five years
options.misconception: treats a fluctuating trend as if it carried no explanatory signal

options.text: Service closure is a plausible structured cause of the low participation in ward B
Turnout figures prove that ward B's voters have lost interest in politics
options.misconception: reads turnout variation as proof about citizens' attitudes

questions.explanation: The coincidence between the evening-service closure and the low figure points to a structured cause tied to service access. The figures alone establish neither vote weight nor citizens' attitudes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a run-off reveals that a first round cannot.
questions.stem: Describe what information a run-off supplies that a first round cannot, and explain why that information changes the bargaining position of the leading candidate.

answer.exemplar: A first round reveals the overall ranking but leaves the top candidate short of a majority, so nobody can claim a mandate. A run-off reveals which of the two leading candidates the wider electorate prefers, because every ballot goes to one of them. That second count removes the ambiguity of the first: the leading candidate can no longer rely on a fragmented opposition to hold a narrow plurality, and must instead assemble the majority of voters who preferred the candidate who now faces them, which typically requires new alliances.

questions.explanation: A run-off produces a majority between two candidates, which a fragmented first round cannot. That removes the leading candidate's ability to rely on a split opposition and forces new alliances.
questions.hint: Compare what each round can demonstrate.

Commissioner: the draft was circulated to all members in January and we have no objection to it. Chair: and the member elected for the northern corridor in that last election? Member: the boundaries are a matter for the commission, and I have nothing further to add.

questions.stem: What does the transcript suggest about how the draft boundaries were handled?

options.misconception: reads the exchange as a suppressed objection from the sitting member

options.text: The commissioner had not received the draft before the hearing began
options.misconception: assumes the absence of comment means the draft was never received

options.text: The commission adopted the draft only after the tribunal confirmed it
options.misconception: believes a tribunal ruling was a precondition for adoption

options.text: The draft circulated in advance, so no single member could shape it alone

questions.explanation: The draft circulated to all members in January and no objection was raised, so the map was not shaped in private by one participant. Silence at a hearing does not show the draft went unreceived.
questions.hint: Note when the draft was circulated.

questions.learningObjective: Order the stages that establish authority to govern.
questions.stem: Which ordering correctly describes how authority to govern is established in a parliamentary system with a directly elected council?

options.text: Election creates representatives, who then form a government and set policy
Policy is agreed first, and the election then selects people to implement it
options.misconception: believes policy commitments are set before voters choose representatives

options.text: Government ministries are appointed first, and the election ratifies their work
options.misconception: reverses the chain by putting ministry appointments ahead of the vote

options.text: A single ballot determines the cabinet, the council and the budget together
options.misconception: assumes one ballot settles the cabinet and the legislature at once

options.text: Constituents in the smallest district receive far less representation per head
Voters in large districts should be given two ballots to compensate them
options.misconception: prescribes extra ballots as the only remedy for unequal districts

options.text: The reviewer would object only if the smallest district were rural
options.misconception: treats urban and rural districts as legally different categories

options.text: U can win the second poll outright because the notice lists three candidates
options.misconception: believes three names on the ballot means three reach the final

options.text: U must contest the second poll because written withdrawal is optional
options.misconception: reads the withdrawal option as compulsory rather than permitted

options.text: U could withdraw and influence the contest between the two leading candidates
U's votes are added to T's total when the second poll is held
options.misconception: assumes first-round votes transfer into the run-off count

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how malapportionment is detected and how partisan advantage is shown.
questions.stem: Explain how a boundary commission can detect malapportionment in a draft map, and state what evidence would be needed to show the malapportionment works in favour of one party.

answer.exemplar: A commission can compute the number of residents per seat in every district and compare them. A district whose population per seat is far above the average is under-represented per head, and one far below is over-represented. To show partisan advantage the evidence must go further: the draft must be compared with the party's previous seat share, the change in population per seat must be large and one-sided, and the timing or drafting record should show that the party knew the outcome it could gain. Inequality alone shows distortion, not a purpose.

questions.explanation: Residents per seat exposes the distortion, but partisan advantage needs extra evidence: a one-sided change tied to one party and a drafting record showing knowledge of the gain.
questions.hint: Inequality is not the same as partisan advantage.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Equal voice against a majority rule
questions.learningObjective: Assess equal voice across a staged consultation design.

stimulus.body: The consultation will run in three stages. First, every registered user is sent a paper ballot with one candidate per district. Second, the results are used to allocate a fixed number of seats per district in proportion to the votes cast in that district. Third, a final stage lets the whole city vote on the draft service map, with the outcome reported but not binding on the council.

questions.stem: Given the three stages, which statement about equal voice holds?

options.text: The final citywide vote overrides the district results and sets the map
options.misconception: believes a non-binding report can still override an earlier binding result

options.text: Every registered user has the same weight because each votes once in stage one
options.misconception: assumes one ballot per voter implies equal weight in the allocation

options.text: Weight varies because votes per seat differ between districts of unequal size
Stage three guarantees identical voting weight for all registered users
options.misconception: believes a reporting stage can equalise the earlier allocation

questions.explanation: Weight per vote depends on how many votes are cast per seat, so districts of unequal size produce different weight even though everyone votes once. A reporting stage cannot equalise the allocation.
questions.hint: Work out votes cast per seat in each district.

questions.learningObjective: Derive per-ballot weight from an identical roll and differing turnout.

options.text: The low-turnout district's voters carry more weight per ballot cast
The high-turnout district's voters are better represented by their councillor
options.misconception: assumes more ballots cast means a stronger claim on the councillor

options.text: Both districts are equally represented because the roll is identical
options.misconception: ignores that identical rolls do not produce identical results per vote

options.text: Turnout differences are corrected automatically by the seat allocation
options.misconception: believes the seat allocation cancels out any turnout gap

options.text: A fresh count of the first-round votes to check the arithmetic
options.misconception: believes a run-off begins with a recount of the original count

options.text: A second contest between A and B, the two candidates with the most votes
The seat to be shared between A and B because neither reached half
options.misconception: assumes a narrow first round leads to a shared seat

options.text: A count of first preferences to see whether C's votes transfer
options.misconception: confuses the run-off with a transferable vote count

questions.explanation: A first round with no majority triggers a head-to-head between the two candidates with the most votes, which here are A and B. Neither a recount, a shared seat, nor a transferable count follows.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the procedural features that insulate a redraw.

stimulus.body: The commission will consult on a draft revision of the district schedule in March, taking written evidence until the end of April. It will then publish a final schedule with reasons for each change in May, and members elected in the current cycle will retain their seats through the next scheduled review.

questions.stem: What does the bulletin tell an observer about how a redraw is insulated from an election result?

options.text: It shows that boundaries will be redrawn immediately after a contested seat
options.misconception: reads the calendar as showing a redraw triggered by a narrow win

options.text: It shows that sitting members may not seek re-election after a redraw
options.misconception: assumes members are excluded from the next election after a redraw

options.text: It shows that the schedule is revised on a published cycle with stated reasons
It shows that final boundaries are decided by the members being reviewed
options.misconception: believes the reviewed members determine the final schedule themselves

questions.explanation: The bulletin sets a consultation and publication timetable with reasons for changes, so the revision follows a published cycle rather than an election result. It says nothing about barring members from standing.
questions.hint: Look for a fixed timetable and written reasons.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an interim arrangement from a formed government.
questions.stem: Explain how a caretaker or interim arrangement differs from a fully formed government, and what authority each one carries.

answer.exemplar: A caretaker arrangement exists to carry out routine business so that public services continue while no majority is established; its authority is deliberately narrow, covering only what cannot be delayed and avoiding new policy commitments or irreversible decisions. A fully formed government emerges when a candidate or coalition commands enough support to be confident it can survive, and it then carries the full authority of the office, including setting priorities, proposing budgets and filling posts. The distinction is one of mandate, not of whether anyone is nominally in office.

questions.explanation: An interim arrangement handles only what cannot wait and avoids new commitments, because it lacks a settled mandate. A formed government has enough support to survive and exercises the full authority of the office.
questions.hint: Distinguish continuity of service from a mandate.

options.text: The third candidate's votes must be redistributed to the winner by rule

options.misconception: treats a plurality win as an invalid result

options.text: Shift workers who cannot vote before 8pm may find no candidate to support

questions.explanation: A single-name contest forces voters to back one of the ward's candidates, so those who cannot attend the polling hours lose the chance to support anyone. The result stays valid and no votes are transferred.

options.misconception: assumes quota rules are advisory and never bind the commission

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a registration deadline can change the balance of power.
questions.stem: Explain why raising the registration deadline can change the balance of power in a close election, and identify the group whose participation is most affected.

answer.exemplar: A registration deadline fixes the electorate before polling day, so votes cast by people who register late are excluded from that contest. Where supporters of one party are more likely to be late registrants, for instance because they are younger, work irregular hours or move between addresses, the deadline removes more of their votes than of anyone else's. That shifts both the totals and the turnout denominator, so the same group can be over-represented in one election and under-represented in the next without any change in its underlying preferences.

questions.explanation: A deadline fixes who can vote, and the people most likely to miss it are not evenly spread across parties, so a change in the rule can move the result. The same group is affected unevenly.
questions.hint: Ask which voters register closest to the deadline.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a widely spread party slate can fail to win seats.
questions.stem: Explain why a rule that lets a minor party nominate one candidate in each of many districts can fail to translate votes into seats, and what determines whether it succeeds.

answer.exemplar: A candidate nominated in a district must win that district, and if every party runs a full slate the votes are spread thinly enough that no candidate reaches the number needed to take the seat. A single party that concentrates its support in a few districts and clears the threshold there can win seats even with a modest national share. What determines success is therefore the concentration of the party's support and the distribution of competing candidates, not the national vote total on its own.

questions.explanation: Seat-winning depends on topping a district, so a widely spread slate can lose everywhere while concentrated support wins some districts. National totals therefore say little on their own about the outcome.
questions.hint: Winning a seat depends on topping one district.

questions.learningObjective: Read a returning officer notice about a run-off and withdrawal.

stimulus.body: No candidate in the depot election has received more than half of the votes cast. Under the rules the two candidates with the highest totals will contest a second poll. Candidates may also request that their names be removed from the second poll ballot, and any such request must be received by the returning officer before noon on the tenth day.

questions.stem: According to the notice, what does the second poll decide and what does it leave open?

options.text: It decides the final tally and leaves open who takes office next year
options.misconception: believes the run-off produces the definitive result of the whole election

options.text: It decides which candidates may register and leaves open the seat totals
options.misconception: confuses a candidate withdrawal with the registration process

options.text: It decides majority support between the two leaders and leaves open who withdrew
It decides the timetable for the next election and leaves open the turnout
options.misconception: assumes the run-off sets the timetable for the next contest

questions.explanation: Because nobody reached half, the notice schedules a contest between the two highest totals, settling majority support between them. Withdrawal is a separate optional step and registration is untouched.
questions.hint: Read which two candidates go to the second poll.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Present both sides of the case for a redraw.
questions.stem: Set out the argument a minister would make to justify a redraw, and then the counter-argument a challenger would make against it.

answer.exemplar: The minister would argue that the existing districts were drawn on population figures that are now out of date, that the services on the network have changed, and that a revision restores a fairer balance between communities, with a published consultation and written reasons showing the process was open. The challenger would answer that the commission redrew the seat shortly after a narrow win in it, that the revised boundaries place the incumbent's supporters in a smaller seat, and that an independent review should test whether the change could have been predicted to help the incumbent.

questions.explanation: The minister rests the case on outdated data and a fairer balance, backed by process safeguards. The challenger answers with timing and effect, arguing the change suited the incumbent and needs scrutiny.
questions.hint: Weigh the minister's data against the challenger's timing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what determines the sequence of items in a meeting.

stimulus.body: Item four: the chair's election. Item five: adoption of the departmental structure. Item six: approval of the appointments put forward by the chair. Item seven: adoption of the annual service plan. The record notes that no item was taken until the certification of the election results had been entered in the minutes.

questions.stem: According to the record, what determines the order in which these items were taken?

options.text: The order in which the members submitted amendments before the meeting
options.misconception: assumes the agenda follows the order members submitted amendments

options.text: The order the chair preferred, since the chair sets the agenda without limit
options.misconception: believes the chair can reorder standing items at will

options.text: The order in which the departments asked for their items to be scheduled
options.misconception: assumes departments control the sequence of business

options.text: A fixed standing order, applied only after the results were certified

questions.explanation: The record shows a standing order applied in sequence after certification of results, so the sequence is rule-bound rather than a matter of preference. Certification is the precondition for the meeting.
questions.hint: A standing order fixes the sequence of items.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess what multi-member districts deliver and leave unresolved.
questions.stem: A city keeps one member per district but introduces a multi-member district in the three largest suburbs. What does the reform deliver and what does it leave?

options.text: More members per district, yet still no guarantee of proportional representation
Proportional representation for the whole city through the three larger districts
options.misconception: assumes multi-member districts automatically deliver proportional results

options.text: A guarantee that every party with five per cent wins a seat
options.misconception: believes a proportional system needs no threshold rule to operate

options.text: The abolition of the first-past-the-post contest in those suburbs
options.misconception: thinks adding members removes the plurality contest in those districts

questions.explanation: Multi-member districts let each member win with a smaller share than in a single-member contest, broadening representation. They do not guarantee that votes and seats match, so proportionality is not assured.
questions.hint: More members per district is not the same as proportionality.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a minor party might want a run-off delayed.
questions.stem: In a run-off election, why might a small party that finished third prefer that the second poll be delayed?

options.text: Because a delay would guarantee that its leader is added to the ballot
options.misconception: assumes delay adds the third candidate to the second ballot

options.text: Because delay gives the leading candidate more time to make damaging commitments
Because the rules require a second poll at least six months after the first
options.misconception: invents a fixed statutory delay that the rules do not contain

options.text: Because the third party would otherwise forfeit its deposits immediately
options.misconception: claims a deposit penalty applies immediately after the first count

questions.explanation: A delay extends the campaign in which the leader must commit to positions the third party can attack, so time can be an asset without a ballot place. The rule adds no third candidate.
questions.hint: Time can change what the leader must promise.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Trace how population change widens a gap between corridors.

stimulus.body: The authority's districts have not been revised since the boundary revision two years ago. Since then the riverside corridor's resident population has fallen by 12 per cent while the hill corridor's has risen by 9 per cent. The note states that no revision is scheduled before the next scheduled review in four years.

questions.stem: What does the census note indicate about representation between the two corridors?

options.text: Both corridors are still represented equally because their seat counts match
options.misconception: assumes matching seat counts still means matching representation

options.text: The hill corridor's residents are now less represented than the riverside ones
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the population change between corridors

options.text: The gap in residents per seat has widened since the last revision
The note proves the boundary schedule was drawn with partisan intent
options.misconception: treats a population shift as evidence of deliberate partisan drawing

questions.explanation: Riverside has lost residents and hill has gained them, so with seat counts unchanged the residents per seat have moved further apart. A demographic shift shows the distortion's direction, not the original intent.
questions.hint: Seat counts have not changed; populations have.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Equal voice against a majority rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one person, one vote is weaker in a district system.
questions.stem: Explain what 'one person, one vote' means when representatives are chosen in districts, and why the phrase is weaker than it sounds.

answer.exemplar: One person, one vote is usually taken to mean that each adult casts a single ballot of equal value. In a district system each person does cast one ballot, but the value of that ballot depends on how many votes are needed to win the seat and how many seats the district has, so a ballot in a small district can carry more weight than a ballot in a large one. The phrase therefore describes equal counting, not equal influence, and the gap between counting and influence is where malapportionment operates.

questions.explanation: Every voter casting one ballot satisfies the counting rule, but influence depends on votes per seat, which differs by district size. The phrase describes equal counting, not equal weight in outcomes.
questions.hint: Counting equality is not the same as weighting.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the relationship a turnout and margin dataset can test.

stimulus.body: Across the last four elections, the two districts with the lowest turnout have also been the two districts where the reported margins were closest, while the two districts with the highest turnout have produced margins above fifteen points. The note adds that turnout has been calculated as ballots cast divided by the registered roll in each district.

questions.stem: Given the note, what relationship between turnout and margins can be tested?

options.text: That high turnout causes voters to vote less consistently between candidates
options.misconception: reverses the relationship by making turnout the dependent variable

options.text: That low turnout guarantees that the eventual winner has a clear majority
options.misconception: assumes low turnout always produces a comfortable majority

options.text: That districts with the same turnout level also show similar reported margins
That margins are a direct measure of how many people found polling difficult
options.misconception: treats margins as a measure of electoral convenience

questions.explanation: The note records turnout and margins for each district, so the claim that similar turnout accompanies similar margins can be checked across the eight districts. Turnout alone explains nothing about voter consistency.
questions.hint: Compare the same measure across districts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the process when a third candidate refuses to withdraw.
questions.stem: A run-off is required and the third candidate refuses to withdraw. What should the board expect from the process?

options.text: A second contest between the top two, with the third candidate outside it
A third round of counting involving all three leading candidates
options.misconception: believes a refusal to withdraw forces another counting round

options.text: A recount of the first round because the third candidate disputes the total
options.misconception: assumes an objection to the total automatically triggers a recount

options.text: A seat shared between the top two since neither won a majority
options.misconception: expects a tie to be resolved by splitting the seat between the leaders

questions.explanation: Refusing to withdraw leaves the third candidate outside the second poll, because the rule names only the two leading candidates. That rule requires no recount, no third round and no shared seat.
questions.hint: The rule names two candidates, not three.
